The 2026 United States Senate election in Iowa will be held on November 3, 2026, to elect a member of the United States Senate to represent the state of Iowa. Republican representative Ashley Hinson and Democratic state representative Josh Turek are the nominees for their respective parties. Republican incumbent Joni Ernst is not seeking a third term.[1]

Primary elections were held on June 2. Endorsed by President Donald Trump, Hinson won the Republican nomination with 73.9% of the vote over former state senator Jim Carlin. Turek won the Democratic nomination with 62.6% of the vote over state senator Zach Wahls.

Democrats have not won a Senate election in Iowa since 2008. This is Iowa's first open Senate election to be held concurrently with an open gubernatorial election since 1968.[2]

Background

[edit]

Since voting for President Barack Obama in both 2008 and 2012, Iowa has trended increasingly Republican and is now considered a moderately to strongly red state at the federal and state level. Republican nominee Donald Trump won Iowa in 2020 by 8 percentage points, and in 2024 grew his margin to 13 percentage points. Republicans control every statewide executive office (except the state auditor's office), majorities in both chambers of the state legislature, and the entire congressional delegation.[3] Incumbent Senator Joni Ernst was first elected as part of the 2014 red wave[4] and was reelected in 2020.[5]

In the latter half of her second term, Ernst came under increasing pressure. In December 2024, she faced pushback from Republicans for her skepticism of Pete Hegseth's nomination for Secretary of Defense.[6] She later sparked controversy for replying "we are all going to die" when a constituent confronted her for deaths that could be caused by cuts to Medicaid and SNAP, which she supported as part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.[7]

In September 2025, Ernst announced that she would not seek reelection, officially citing family obligations, although her decision was interpreted in light of previous controversies. The resulting open seat was expected to make the race more competitive.[8][9]

Libertarian primary

[edit]

On June 2, the Laehn campaign submitted nearly 10,000 signatures to the Iowa Secretary of State, satisfying the 3,500 signature requirement to qualify for the ballot.[80] Laehn was added to the candidate list as the Libertarian Party's candidate.[81]

General election

[edit]

According to The Daily Iowan, the cost of living, inflation, tariffs, health-care affordability, agriculture, and AI data centers are contested issues of the campaign.[83] Debates focused on which candidate was most capable to handle the American affordability crisis.[83][84] Turek has said he would reverse the Medicaid spending cuts passed under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.[85][86][87][88] Hinson supported the cuts as fiscally responsible as well as Trump's tariffs.[83]

Hinson ran on socially conservative policies, opposing a legal right to have an abortion with exceptions for rape, incest, and the life of the mother and LGBTQ movements.[84][89] Turek supports restoring the abortion protections that Roe v. Wade previously provided, by passing a federal law.[85] He claimed that Iowa's six-week abortion ban reduced OB-GYN services available.[85] Turek affirmed conservative policies on guns, transgender rights, and immigration.[84][90]

Turek criticized the concentration of artificial intelligence technology in the hands of a few companies. He supports regulating data centers, opposes tax breaks for their operators, and "safeguards" for the technology.[91][92][93] Hinson is in favor of AI development, and says that preparation for workers is necessary to adapt to AI job losses. She said an "AI economy" is necessary to win an American-Chinese AI arms race, "because the truth is: if we don't, China will."[94][95]
